summary: An addendum to RFC 4348 that updates the RTP payload format for the VMR-WB speech codec to support VMR-WB mode 4. The updates do not affect the modes already specified. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: A small patch to the way a voice codec's packets are packed so a new setting works, without changing the old ones.

subtitle: A small update to the RTP payload format for the VMR-WB speech codec so it can carry the new mode 4.

tldr.problem: The VMR-WB speech codec gained a new operating mode, mode 4, that runs at lower average data rates, but the RTP payload format in RFC 4348 had no entries for it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4424 updates three tables in RFC 4348 by filling reserved entries: two new Codec Mode Request values, three new frame types, and the extra rates. It also lets the mode-set parameter include value 4.
tldr.outcome: Mode 4 can be used with the same payload formats, rules and media type as before, and the existing modes are not affected. The RFC updates RFC 4348.

today: RFC 4424 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4348, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is read together with RFC 4348.

sections.title: An Addendum to RFC 4348
sections.content:
This document is an addendum to RFC 4348. It contains the updates needed to support the new operating mode of the 3GPP2 VMR-WB standard, called VMR-WB mode 4.

Mode 4 runs at a lower data rate but has similar characteristics to the existing modes, such as variable bit rate, narrowband and wideband processing, and continuous and discontinuous transmission. For that reason all provisions and restrictions of RFC 4348 apply to every mode including the new one, and no new media type registration is required.

The file format for storing VMR-WB data covers the new mode as well, and is specified outside this RFC.
sections.eli5: This is a short add-on page to an existing rulebook. The new setting follows the same rules, so almost nothing needs to change.

sections.title: What VMR-WB Is and What Changed
sections.content:
VMR-WB is a wideband speech-coding standard developed by 3GPP2 for encoding and decoding wideband and narrowband speech in multimedia services on 3G CDMA cellular systems. It is source-controlled and variable-rate, with several operating modes. Each mode trades voice quality against average data rate, and the mode is chosen based on network traffic conditions and the desired quality of service.

The new mode works at lower average data rates, which improves system capacity in IP and non-IP networks. To add it, certain reserved table entries in RFC 4348 are used. The existing entries, such as the frame types, stay unchanged, and the original modes are not affected.

Because RFC 4348 already allowed for future extensions, the addition does not affect interoperability with earlier implementations. Implementation, congestion control and security provisions stay identical to RFC 4348.
sections.eli5: The codec is like a dimmer for voice quality. The new setting uses less data, and it fits into a slot that was left empty on purpose.

sections.title: Rates and Mode Requests
sections.content:
Table 1 of RFC 4348 lists the frame types permitted on a CDMA2000 system with their sizes and encoding rates. RFC 4424 replaces it with a table that adds the new permissible rates, which correspond to CDMA2000 rate-set I. Examples are a 171-bit full-rate frame at 8.55 kbps and a 16-bit eighth-rate frame at 0.8 kbps.

Table 2 of RFC 4348 maps Codec Mode Request (CMR) values to VMR-WB operating modes. The update adds CMR value 7 for VMR-WB mode 4 and CMR value 8 for mode 4 with maximum half-rate encoding. These replace values that were reserved. CMR 15 still means no preference, and 9 to 14 stay reserved.
sections.eli5: A mode request is a number you hold up to ask for a setting. Numbers 7 and 8 used to be blank, and now they ask for the new setting.

sections.title: New Frame Types
sections.content:
Table 3 of RFC 4348 lists the payload frame types (FTs) for real-time transport. The update fills three reserved entries: FT 7 is full-rate at 8.55 kbps with 171 bits, FT 8 is half-rate at 4.0 kbps with 80 bits, and FT 10 is eighth-rate at 0.8 kbps with 16 bits. Existing entries do not change.

The RFC points out that the frame sizes are unique and different, which allows a header-free payload format for all modes of operation.
sections.eli5: Every kind of voice packet has a different size, so the receiver can tell which kind it got just by measuring it. The new kinds have new sizes.

sections.title: Negotiating Mode 4
sections.content: The mode-set MIME parameter value 4 is defined to show that VMR-WB mode 4 is supported and used. The active modes are negotiated and agreed by the IP terminals through the offer/answer model in Section 9.3 of RFC 4348.
sections.eli5: Two phones agree on which settings they will both use before they start talking, and now setting 4 can be on that list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section is a single line: the considerations are the same as in RFC 4348. The introduction to the update also says that implementation, congestion control and security provisions are identical to that RFC.
sections.eli5: Nothing new is risky here, so the safety rules from the older rulebook still apply.

sections.title: Changes to the Media Type Registration
sections.content:
This document updates the media type registered by RFC 4348. IANA added this RFC as a reference to that registration and modified the optional mode-set parameter.

The registration text changes from modes 0, 1, 2 and 3 to modes 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4, and from the set 0 to 3 to the set 0 to 4. The original VMR-WB document is 3GPP2 C.S0052-A v1.0, and RFC 4424 is IANA's second reference.
sections.eli5: The official list of allowed settings was edited so that setting 4 is now written on it.
